name: Cascade Failure
subtitle: Blackwood Water Authority
tagline: The tank overflowed. Every screen said it couldn't.
intro:
At 02:00 on a quiet night, Tank T-101 at the Blackwood Water Authority treatment plant overflowed. The HMI showed a steady 5 m the whole time. The historian agrees. The Safety Instrumented System, the last line of defence, never tripped and never raised an alarm.

You are the OT incident responder called in at dawn. You have an edge SPAN capture, a historian export, the SIS controller's compiled logic, and access to the plant's engineering workstation and simulators. Somebody walked through the DMZ, blinded the operators, silenced the safety system and left something behind in the PLC.

Find out who, how, and what they left. Then get the plant back.

acts.name: The Breach
acts.blurb: Every malicious session came from the DMZ proxy. Nobody lives on a proxy.

acts.name: Blind Operators
acts.blurb: The screens were lying, and the safety system kept quiet.

acts.name: Ghost in the Logic
acts.blurb: The PLC is running more than the project shows.

acts.name: The Cascade
acts.blurb: Replay the attack end to end, and hear what the pump was saying.

acts.name: Recovery
acts.blurb: Fail over to a clean standby, if you can keep it clean.

chapters.name: The Leaky Hop
chapters.description:
At 02:17 UTC someone wrote new setpoints to **PLC-01** at the Blackwood Water Authority treatment plant. Every malicious Modbus and OPC UA session in the edge SPAN capture comes from the DMZ proxy `192.168.20.9`, so the proxy is all the firewall logs show.

A proxy only relays the stream it is given. Find the host that is really behind it.

Submit the attacker's real IPv4 address as `HXN{a.b.c.d}`.
hints: A TCP relay carries bytes, not name lookups. Who had to resolve the PLC's hostname just before the proxy connected?
Several hosts resolve `plc01` legitimately. Rule out every resolver that then talks to the PLC directly, and check the OPC UA ApplicationUri.

story.open:
“Firewall says it was the DMZ proxy. Every write, every session.”
“The proxy didn’t wake up at two in the morning and decide to flood a tank.”
“So who was driving it?”
“Someone who thought a proxy was enough to hide behind.”

The edge SPAN capture covers the minutes around the first malicious write to PLC-01. It is noisy: HMIs, the historian, the engineering workstation and a vendor subnet all talking at once.

Proxies forward bytes. They don’t always forward everything.
story.close:
One host on the vendor subnet resolved the PLC’s name a heartbeat before the proxy connected, and its name is written into the proxied OPC UA session too.

“That’s our operator.”
“Then what were they doing for the half hour before the writes?”

chapters.name: The Impossible Levels
chapters.description:
During the intrusion the operators at HMI-01 watched Tank T-101 sit calmly near 5 m. The historian export agrees with them and the flows even balance. Engineering says the tank overflowed anyway.

Using the historian export and the pump datasheet, rebuild the true level from physics and find the largest gap between the real level and what the HMI showed.

Submit the peak deviation in metres, rounded to 2 decimals: `HXN{x.xx}`.
hints: Read the datasheet closely: what does a stopped fixed-speed pump with a check valve actually move? Is its discharge even metered?
Trust only measured quantities. Integrate `dh = (Qin - Qout) * dt / A` with the tank geometry from the datasheet.

story.open:
“The night shift swears the level never moved.”
“The historian backs them up. Inflow in, outflow out. Perfectly balanced.”
“Then why is there water on the floor of the pump house?”

You have the historian export for T-101 and the datasheet for the outlet pump. The numbers add up. That is the problem.
story.close:
The HMI froze on its last good value while the real level climbed metres above it, and the “balanced” outflow came from a pump that was logged as stopped.

“The operators weren’t asleep. They were blind.”
“A tank that high should have tripped the SIS. Why didn’t it?”

chapters.name: The Silent Safety System
chapters.description:
The level hit its HiHi trip point and the Safety Instrumented System did nothing. It did it quietly, with no alarm on the DCS. We pulled the compiled safety program from the SIS controller along with the vendor's image-format reference card.

Disassemble the logic and find the bypass the attacker used. Submit its tag exactly as the controller emits it: `HXN{TAG}`.
hints: `strings` shows several candidate tags and constants. Some are decoys. Disassemble it properly with the opcode card.
Look for a path that suppresses the trip *without* raising an alarm, and make sure the code you read is actually reachable.

story.open:
“The SIS is independent. Separate controller, separate transmitters. It can’t be fooled by the HMI.”
“It wasn’t fooled. It was told to stand down.”
“There’d be an alarm. Every bypass is annunciated.”
“Every bypass the vendor wrote.”

The safety program has been pulled from the controller along with the vendor’s image-format card. Somewhere in a few hundred bytes is the reason the plant didn’t trip.
story.close:
A second bypass suppresses the trip and says nothing to the DCS. Its diagnostic word is one you will see again.

“They knew this system well.”
“Well enough to leave something in the PLC too?”

chapters.name: Ghost Rung
chapters.description:
The engineering workstation shows PLC-01's ladder project as two clean, harmless rungs. The PLC is running something else.

Open the simulator, find the logic the project doesn't show, work out what triggers it, and make it fire. The hidden rung writes an implant configuration into memory, and the simulator shows the flag once the rung really executes.

Simulator: [https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/ghost-rung/](https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/ghost-rung/)

Flag format: `HXN{config}`. You will need the diagnostic word from *The Silent Safety System*.
hints: Compare the online program with the offline project. Is there a block the project doesn't list?
Decode the block's bytes with the opcode card. Every condition has to be true in the **same scan**, timer and counter included.

deployment.notes: Browser simulator in sim-site/, published by scripts/build_api.py to https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/ghost-rung/. To run locally: cd sim-site && python -m http.server 8080, then open http://localhost:8080 (WebCrypto needs localhost or https).

story.open:
“Project’s clean. Two rungs, exactly what we commissioned.”
“That’s the copy on your laptop. What’s on the controller?”
“...The same thing. Isn’t it?”

The engineering workstation can compare what it thinks the PLC runs with what the PLC actually holds. Something there doesn’t match, and it is waiting for the right conditions before it does anything.
story.close:
The hidden rung fires and writes out its configuration in plain ASCII: the trigger level, the pump it drives, and the data block it lives in.

“It wasn’t only flooding the tank.”
“No. When the level hit its mark, it was supposed to start talking.”

chapters.name: Cascade Complete
chapters.description:
You now know the attacker's source, the SIS bypass and the implant config. Replay the whole attack against the plant simulator: keep the operators blind, defeat the safety system and drive the tank to the implant's trigger level.

Once triggered, the implant exfiltrates a message by switching a pump on and off. The message is in the tank level itself. Capture the level transmitter samples and decode it.

Simulator: [https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/cascade-complete/](https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/cascade-complete/)

Needs the answers from **The Leaky Hop**,** The Silent Safety System **and** Ghost Rung**. No banner appears here: submit the decoded ASCII as `HXN{MESSAGE}`.
hints: The console has a `help` and a `regs` command. If the operators can still see the real level, they will stop you.
A pump running drains the tank and a stopped pump lets it fill. The bits are encoded in the transitions, not the levels: think line coding.

deployment.notes: Browser simulator in sim-site/, published by scripts/build_api.py to https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/cascade-complete/. To run locally: cd sim-site && python -m http.server 8080, then open http://localhost:8080 (WebCrypto needs localhost or https).

story.open:
“We know the source, the bypass and the implant. What we don’t know is what it sent.”
“Sent how? It never touched the internet.”
“It didn’t need to. It had a pump and a level transmitter.”

Replay the night on the plant simulator, step by step, as the attacker did. Keep the HMI blind, keep the SIS quiet and push the tank to the trigger. Then watch the level and write down what it does.
story.close:
Decoded from the rise and fall of LT-101, the message is a two-word status report: the attacker’s confirmation that the job was done.

“So they got their proof.”
“And left the implant behind to do it again. Now we take the plant back.”

chapters.name: Hot Standby
chapters.description:
Recovery time. PLC-01 runs as a redundant pair: the primary syncs its `%DB10` parameter block to a hot standby every 15 seconds, and the plan is to fail over to a clean standby.

The attacker poisoned `%DB10`, and not all in the same way. Restore every value to its design basis, get a clean copy onto the standby, and fail over. If the standby holds the plant stable for 60 seconds, the recovery token is released.

Simulator: [https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/hot-standby/](https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/hot-standby/)

Flag format: `HXN{token}`. The correct block is not in the page: you have to work it out.
hints: Each slot is an IEEE-754 REAL stored as two 16-bit words. Try every byte and word order (ABCD, CDAB, BADC, DCBA) and ask which value makes engineering sense.
Watch the event log around each sync. You are not the only one writing to `%DB10`.

deployment.notes: Browser simulator in sim-site/, published by scripts/build_api.py to https://a-y-u-s-h-y-a.github.io/project-haxnation/sims/hot-standby/. To run locally: cd sim-site && python -m http.server 8080, then open http://localhost:8080 (WebCrypto needs localhost or https).

story.open:
“PLC-01 has a hot standby. Fail over and we’re clean.”
“The standby syncs from the primary every fifteen seconds.”
“So?”
“So it has a perfect copy of everything they poisoned.”

The parameter block %DB10 has been tampered with, slot by slot, and each slot in a different way. Fix it, get a clean copy onto the standby and fail over. Something on the network still has write access.
story.close: The standby takes control with a clean block, rides out the morning inflow surge and holds steady. The recovery token comes back.

finale.title: Cascade Contained
finale.text:
“Start to finish.”
“A vendor-subnet host behind the DMZ proxy. A frozen HMI and forged flows. A silent SIS bypass. A ghost rung in the PLC that turned a pump into a radio. And an implant that kept re-poisoning the block we were trying to fail over to.”
“Any one of those alone, and somebody notices.”
“That’s why they chained them.”

The proxy route is shut, the SIS logic is restored from a verified baseline, %DB99 is gone and both controllers carry a clean %DB10. T-101 runs at 5 m, and this time the screen is telling the truth.

The case file is closed. Your name is on it.
